speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: BANK OF MONTREAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Finance which I asked yesterday in his absence. First, will the minister comment on the dispatch in yesterday morning's Gazette stating that Mr. Gordon Ball, president of the Bank of Montreal, has called on the government for a prompt "public announcement that no fundamental changes in the Canadian banking structure are contemplated without the fullest possible investigation of what might be involved"? Second, will the minister say what form of investigation will take place? Third, can the minister comment on the statement in the Gazette dispatch which says that Mr. Ball "has approached Finance Minister Harris about Mr. Coyne's proposals outlined in the Bank of Canada's report earlier this month"?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BANK OF MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman asked this question yesterday. I was regrettably absent, but I was notified of it by my staff. Later in the day, I issued a statement to the press which hon. members might have seen, but which I feel I should read into the record. The statement is made in this form:
I have not seen the text of Mr. Ball's statement, nor has a copy yet reached my office. I have, however, seen extracts which have appeared in today's newspapers.
In his annual report, the governor of the Bank of Canada made a reference to the wide fluctuations in the chartered banks' general loans as well as in their investments in longer-term securities and in insured housing mortgages, and expressed the view that it would be desirable to explore means of encouraging a greater degree of stability and continuity in these forms of investment. He made it plain both in his report and in prior and subsequent talks with the top officials of the chartered banks that no radical, fundamental or early changes in the banking structure were contemplated. He went on to say in his report that "the possibility of a gradual approach" toward making some distinction between personal savings and the commercial lending field "would seem to be worthy of study
and discussion". The approach suggested for discussion, as I understand it, would reduce rather than increase the central bank's present influence over savings deposits which are at present of necessity treated in the same way as commercial deposits.
In any case no "radical", "fundamental" or "precipitate" actions relating to the structure of Canadian banking have been suggested, nor are they contemplated by the government.
I think that is sufficient comment, Mr. Speaker, on the statement issued by the president of the Bank of Montreal. In answer to the other question asked as to the approach that the president made to me, I may say that approach consisted of a statement by Mr. Ball that he felt the question that the hon. member for Greenwood asked of me earlier this month, and my answer, in which I said that any discussion of this kind and any changes would be recommended by the government, if by anyone, in the normal way of amendments to the Bank Act, had not sufficiently emphasized the fact that none of these things could occur without government recommendation to the House of Commons, followed by action of the house in either accepting or rejecting these proposed amendments. I wish, therefore, to make it quite clear that what has happened is that the governor of the bank has suggested for discussion certain questions and that the government does not intend to make recommendations along those lines to the House of Commons. Should any recommendations of that kind be made on future occasions, they would be subject to full discussion both in the house and in the banking and commerce committee, and would have to be taken by way of amendments to the Bank Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FISHERIES CONCERNING FEDERAL AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of members have given me notice of their intention to ask questions about the same subject. They were the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Jones), the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud).
I believe, sir, that the best way to deal with all these questions is to read into Hansard the text of the statement which was handed to the press in Vancouver yesterday by the Minister of Fisheries. Before reading this statement I should say I have learned from the Minister of Fisheries this morning that in his statement he never mentioned any figure of expenditures, and particularly the figure of $300 million. If I can have your indulgence to read it, sir, here is the statement:
In 1955 parliament passed the International River Improvements Act giving the federal government jurisdiction over works constructed on rivers crossing the international boundary, and over the flow of water from these rivers across the boundary. The purpose of the act is to assure maximum power development in Canada from such rivers, and maximum power return to Canada from downstream power development in the United States as a consequence of water storage in Canada.
The international joint commission has endeavoured to negotiate an agreement on the division of these downstream benefits, but little progress has been made. To expedite a settlement, the government of Canada and the government of the United States entered into direct negotiations at Ottawa on March 19 this year. An early agreement will speed up industrial development in both British Columbia and the northwest states, and will save the Fraser river fisheries from the threat of power development.
Once agreement is reached on the division of power between the two countries, it will be the responsibility of the provincial government of British Columbia to decide whether privately owned or publicly owned agencies are to develop this power on the Canadian side, and to distribute the power received from the United States in return for downstream benefits derived from Canadian water storage.
This project will be a vast one, entailing large-scale investment. Normally power development within a province is the responsibility of the provincial government. Parliament, however, has given the federal government a measure of jurisdiction over the Columbia river as an international stream, so the federal government has a measure of responsibility, too, which it has accepted so far by spending almost $5 million on engineering surveys.
If, after international agreement has been reached, the provincial government should decide

on public development of this great power potential and need assistance in financing, the federal government will be prepared to assist in the same way that it has joined with the government of Ontario in constructing the interprovincial gas pipe line across northern Ontario, and has offered to assist the governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to build an interprovincial power grid linking the thermal power plants of Nova Scotia with the hydroelectric power plants of New Brunswick. Such assistance is not indirect, by way of subsidies, grants or guarantee of bonds, but by direct participation either in joint crown companies or federal crown companies doing specific sections of the development. Since this project will unquestionably be self-liquidating the provincial government can over the years buy out the federal government's interests in the usual way.
The most obvious advantage in this course is the fact that the federal government can finance such work at considerably less interest charges than either the provincial government or private power companies, with consequent savings to the consumer.
This is but another example of the way the federal government is willing to encourage sound economic development in every part of the nation.
I should add one word. It is that when the Minister of Fisheries speaks of linking the thermal power plants of Nova Scotia with the hydroelectric power plants of New Brunswick he is oversimplifying it a little. In both provinces you find both sorts of plants, and the aim is to link them. I should also add that it should not be understood from this statement that the possibility of the diversion of the Columbia river to the Fraser river has been abandoned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is no secret, I am sure, that many such representations have been made to the government and to myself as Minister of Justice. The position we have always taken I think may be expressed in these terms which I have used in replying to various people who had written to me in this connection. The parliament of Canada first enacted laws prohibiting the use of trading stamps in Canada over half a century ago in the year 1905. When recently in 1954 the parliament of Canada enacted the first over-all consolidation of the Criminal Code parliament retained in this new consolidation the law against trading stamps which had been enacted in 1905 and has been in effect ever since. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that the information that was asked for and should have been available when the resolution was considered in committee on March 14 is not available now. It was understood that it would be available now and it ought to be available now so that so far as it calls for discussion on the second reading there would be full opportunity now to review it and discuss it.
Sir, the resolution preceding the introduction of this bill was considered in committee on March 13 and 14. The bill conforms with
the resolution which, following a division of

Grain
the house, was reported and the bill introduced. So far as Her Majesty's loyal opposition is concerned, our position with respect to the measure was stated at the resolution stage and is a matter of record in Hansard of March 13 and 14.
It is the same position that this party took when the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act was under discussion in this house a year ago and it is the position which we had taken for years prior to that. Our position and policy is one in favour of cash advances on farm-stored western wheat.
The minister in his opening statement on March 13 admitted that only limited use has been made of the facilities available under the act. The limited use is best illustrated by the further information elicited from the minister as reported at page 2202 of Hansard of March 14 when he said in reply to questions:
The loans in the first year of operation were 10,326 for an amount of $7,893,830.32. In the second year, up to January 31, 1957, the number of loans totalled 5,034 for an amount of $3,498,011.67.
I asked at that time for a statement as to the distribution of these loans among the three western provinces, but that information was not forthcoming. It is quite evident by simple arithmetical calculation that the average loan in the first year the act was in effect was $766. In the current year the average loan is $695.
We are not in a position to judge the significance of the increase in the maximum loan intended by the present bill from $1,500 to $3,000 because the question I asked on that occasion as to the number of loans of the maximum amount under the present act, namely $1,500, was not answered. The minister did not have that information so the house is hardly in a position to judge now whether there is any particular efficacy or value promised by the amendment which now proposes to increase the permissible maximum loan from $1,500 to $3,000.
Sir, the problem remains and can be very simply stated. Western Canada is suffering from a cash shortage. At the same time western Canada has a huge accumulated surplus of unmarketed wheat which can only be marketed through the Canadian wheat board. In the face of this situation and this continuing problem the policy of Her Majesty's loyal opposition is one in favour of cash advances on farm-stored wheat.
That position was clearly stated by the Leader of the Opposition, speaking in the discussion at the resolution stage when with reference to the policy that we advocate he said, as reported at page 2188 of Hansard of March 14:
It is recommended by the Gordon commission; it is demanded by various farm organizations other 
than the farm union; it is something which can be brought into effect without the possibility of loss, for there is only one market in which the farmer can sell his wheat.
And further, at page 2189, he stated the policy of the Conservative party in these words:
We believe that the only salvation for the western farmer, with his markets lost and his wheat therefore unmarketable, is that there should be cash advances. Second, we believe that every encouragement should be given to the farmer to provide his own storage, and that in the provision of such storage additional write-offs should be permitted when determining the amount of his income tax. We believe that under proper circumstances there should be provision for cash advances on farm-stored grain similar to the system in effect in the United States.
There is one other feature of the present bill which also makes it unpalatable to Her Majesty's loyal opposition. The present act fixes a ceiling upon the rate of interest which may be charged upon bank loans to qualify for government guarantees. That maximum interest rate is 5 per cent. Indeed, when the measure was under discussion in this house a year ago the opposition took issue even with a maximum as high as 5 per cent having regard to the fact that a government guarantee was to be attached to the loans.
The government now proposes to remove that maximum and I ask the house to give serious consideration to the effect of the removal of that maximum. The reason is perfectly clear. The inevitable result and the obvious intention of the government in proposing the removal of that maximum is that the interest rate may be raised.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce at the resolution stage engaged in a lot of transparent quibbling and shilly-shallying on this subject. He was invited to make a frank statement as to the real reason and purpose behind the proposal for removal of the maximum and in the midst of his quibbles the suggestion was made that there would be great uncertainty and no one could determine at this stage what the interest rate might be six months hence. Sir, that is not the point at all. The minister said, as reported at page 2202 of Hansard:
Frankly, the government feels that this is not the time to establish a maximum rate for a period that begins some months hence.
He said further, as reported at page 2203:
... I think any man would be foolish to negotiate today for a rate which will apply next autumn and which might be obtainable at a lower figure at that time.
There is a first class example of governmental shilly-shallying, for all that the act does today is to fix the maximum. There is nothing today to prevent a government guarantee of such a loan at a lower rate of

interest than 5 per cent if it conforms with the other requirements established by the act. The only purpose that could be served by the removal of the statutory maximum is to permit an increase in the rate and that is why I say the minister's remarks on this subject were transparent shilly-shallying.
The minister also said, as reported at page 2203:
I hope the interest rate will go down.
And later he said:
I am hoping we will get a lower interest rate by autumn.
If the prospect is for a lower interest rate there is no need to remove the maximum now fixed by the act upon the interest rate. I do not think that any person is likely to be fooled by this kind of shilly-shallying to which we have become long accustomed. The only reason that could prompt the government to propose the removal of that maximum is that they are fully expecting and contemplating an increase in the interest rate. They accept the fact and are now proposing to remove from the act the one fetter that there is upon the interest rate. The maximum is going to be removed entirely by the present bill. That is an additional reason for us to dislike the bill, and even if that feature stood alone it would be sufficient reason for us to dislike the bill.
Our position on the charging of interest on advances was stated by the Leader of the Opposition in speaking on March 14, as reported at page 2189, when he said:
Here the farmers find themselves once more handed a proposition requiring them to pay interest on their earnings.
Later on he said:
There was no justification for interest being paid in the first place, and there is no justification for an additional amount being paid.
Our position is unchanged. We believe in cash advances on farm stored wheat as the only policy to meet the needs of western Canada and the continuing problem that is created there by reason of the failure of the government agency to sell the accumulated surplus of wheat.
Instead the approach of this bill is all wrong. This is the kind of bill that ought not to have been brought forward. The kind of bill we asked for last year and are continuing to ask for now is one that will grapple effectively and sensibly and realistically with the problem. Such a bill should make provision for cash advances an farm-stored wheat. For these reasons we oppose the bill.

I think the hon. member must be pretty naive when he suggests that at this time we are discussing something which is not of tremendous importance and that the details could be better discussed in committee. That may be true, but if we give second reading to this bill we are giving our nod to the bill.
It is rather interesting to hear the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) speak on behalf of the official opposition. It would appear as though he has replaced the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) as the agricultural expert of the official opposition. However, it would appear to me that the hon. member is not fully acquainted with farm problems and this is indicated when he speaks about cash advances. On reflection I think he will agree that when the official opposition is proposing cash advances those cash advances should be on farm-stored grain and not confined to wheat. It should be the right of the farmer to make application for a loan as indicated by the farm organizations.

speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for the clarification of his statement. We in this party have always believed that the farmer is entitled to cash advances on farm-stored grain. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) introduced the resolution preceding this bill he gave the house his conception of the legislation in the following words, as reported on page 2196 of Hansard of March 14 as follows:
Mr. Chairman, there seems to be a misconception about what we are trying to do. It has been assumed that the bill to follow this resolution will change the complexion of western agriculture from being in the distressed state in which we are told it is now, to a state of great prosperity.
In my opinion that is the understatement of the year. I was concerned that no private members of the Liberal party rose to their feet during the resolution stage and took part in this important debate. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is thousands of miles away and I suggest that this would be a good opportunity for them to participate in this debate and say what they think in

Grain
respect to cash advances and this bill which in effect permits the farmer who has produced grain to go to the bank, make his statement and then after practically getting down on his knees get an advance on his year's work.
So far the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Mang) who sits over yonder has not taken part in this debate, and neither have the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer), the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) and the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). I believe that those hon. members would have ideas in connection with this important matter and they should get up on their feet during the closing days of this session and place those ideas on the record and indicate their support of us who are trying honestly to place the problems of the western farmer before this house. Their inactivity, their apparent complacency and political impotency have resulted in other hon. members, particularly those from eastern Canada, not being able to appreciate the plight of the farmer, particularly the farmer in the west. I suggest to the hon. members that in the next day or two they get up and express themselves on this important legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
The
hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) says "without fear of retaliation". I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce has to some extent used the big stick in this house. When he introduced the resolution he said he was going to place this legislation before the house to see how it went. We in this group are glad to help expedite this legislation, but we do not want this house or any member in it to have a false conception about how we feel about this legislation. We think it is a third-rate answer to the request of organized agriculture throughout Canada. It is not true, as was indicated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he introduced the resolution, that this legislation conforms to the will of organized agriculture throughout Canada. Nothing could be further from the truth. This is simply a death-bed acceptance by organized agriculture of an opportunity to get some cash into the farmer's hands.
There would appear to be a misapprehension throughout Canada in respect to what we and other members of this house who sometimes speak on behalf of agriculture, particularly western agriculture, think should be done. Some hon. members appear to think of the farmers as asking for a hand-out. Nothing could be further from the truth. I remember in an earlier debate this session

the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking) made the statement that beggars cannot always be choosers in connection with wheat. The farmers are not beggars. All they are asking is that they be given a fair and equitable deal. I have a bone of contention to pick with some of these people who sit in high ivory towers. I have here an article which appeared in the Leader-Post. Reference is made in this article to an address made by Dean A. G. McCalla of the University of Alberta faculty of agriculture in which he is reported to have used very blunt language to a farm organization. Dean McCalla is reported to have said:
Behind the demands of the militant farm organizations is the assumption that farming is a special, almost sacred "way of life"; that those who follow it deserve special treatment; that the state should carry them if they cannot make their farms pay.
I am greatly surprised that an educated person would make such a statement. The farmers do not want to be in a special category. As a matter of fact they have been the forgotten people throughout the years as far as successive federal governments are concerned. As far as we are concerned we want to put on the record that it was only after the farmers of western Canada plowed the wheat fields and began the production of agricultural commodities that other parts of Canada became prosperous. We are happy to have that state of affairs and when we are asking for justice and policies which would incidentally benefit all Canada we do not want to be classified as peasants or beggars looking for hand-outs.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that farmers' delegations coming to Ottawa usually get a fine reception from all parties and from the cabinet, and perhaps they go home feeling elated and thinking they have left a good impression. Very likely they believe that as a result of that they can expect some just and fair consideration of their problems. I have here a clipping from the Star-Phoenix of March 19, 1957, headed:	"Harris Impressed, But Budget Does Not Show It." I just want to quote one short paragraph:
R. V. Mitchell, Blucher, a member of the recent farm union delegation which presented a brief on agriculture to the federal cabinet, said Mr. Harris had remarked to the delegation that there was "no segment of Canada more in need of fair treatment than the prairies". However, when his budget came out it appeared he had forgotten this opinion.
That is how it seems to some of us, Mr. Speaker. We have received a lot of sympathy; we have received many indications from people in important government positions that they know the farmers' problems;

but we have nothing forthcoming of an important legislative nature by means of which those problems could be solved.
Under the legislation before the house today it is proposed that farmers who go to the banks may be granted loans, after they have committed themselves and made financial statements, at the discretion of the banker. I think all farm organizations will agree that the present legislation does not entitle any farmer to a loan; it will still be a matter for the banker concerned to decide whether or not any particular farmer should get a loan. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this legislation is completely inadequate.
But before I go into the merits or demerits of this specific proposal I would like to indicate some of the problems which face farmers at the present time. Just the other day I had a letter from a farmer who lives about 50 miles from my home, and he intimated that at this date 75 per cent of the crop is still on the farm. As a matter of fact, one-third of all marketing points in Saskatchewan are still on a two-bushel quota. That means that these farmers, as far as the sale of their grain is concerned, have only a few hundred dollars with which to carry on. This problem confronts the businessmen as well as the farmers and it is distressing to go into various towns of western Canada and see business people who have tried to carry on with large unpaid accounts on their books-people who have tried to "carry" a lot of these farmers without interest charges in an effort to help them in a difficult situation. Some of these businesses are going into liquidation because they cannot get any credit from the wholesalers, since they, too, are "on the spot".
Mr. Speaker, we have stated over the years that we need permanent legislation to meet this problem. We need it because the situation has been such, in the last five or six years, that there is a great carry-over from year to year of the farmers' grain. I would like to point out to the house that whether a farmer is securely established or not it takes about $500 to store 1,000 bushels of grain properly on a farm. If the grain is put into cheap or improper storage it is likely there will be a tremendous loss on that grain. In my opinion it takes 15 or 20 years of good farming before a farmer can put himself into a financial position where he can store a full crop on his farm and be able to finance it himself. The young farmer, the veteran coming back from a war, is in no position to do that sort of thing. Thus, we have the problem of building proper storage facilities in which to house the grain until it can be sold.
Grain
In connection with this, the minister said at the outset of his remarks, when he introduced the resolution prefacing this bill, that this measure had quite completely met the requests of organized agriculture in Canada, and he added that he was very happy that such was the case because he had never brought before parliament a bill which he felt was more in line with what had been demanded by the farm organizations. Well, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that this is not the case. Here is a letter which was addressed to Mr. Zaplitny by Mr. Rudolph Usick, a Manitoba farm union official, and I wish to quote a portion of it. He says this:
Since the prairie grain producers interim financing act is up for amendment in the House of Commons I thought I should mention a meeting of ten organizations held in Saskatoon on Friday, March 1.
These ten represented the three pools, the three federations of agriculture of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta and the United Grain Growers.
At this meeting a resolution was passed and sent by telegram to Messrs. Howe, Gardiner, Harris and St. Laurent. No press release was issued because they wanted the government to have an opportunity to study the proposals.
Further on, the letter says:
It was because we could not agree on a united plan of cash advances that the following resolution was passed:
Resolved, that while we do not agree that the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act is the most satisfactory method for making money available on grain that cannot be delivered, however in view of the late date in having a more satisfactory plan for cash advances adopted at this session of parliament this committee recommends to the federal government the inclusion of the following amendments:
I am going to read this, Mr. Speaker, because these amendments are important, and they are in no way in conformity with what this bill proposes.
a.	That the basis for loans be set at $4 per specified acre up to a maximum of 800 acres.
That would mean, Mr. Speaker, that there would be a maximum loan of $3,200. And this is the only clause of the resolution that the bill conforms with:
b.	That the time for advancement of loans be set ahead to September 1.
It continues:
c.	That credit unions and treasury branches be empowered to advance loans.
d.	That interest rates be as low as possible, and in any event not higher than those paid by the Canadian wheat board.
This bill, of course, proposes that the interest rate should be set by order in council, and there can only be one reason for that provision being in the bill, namely, that there is a great possibility that the interest rate will be higher.

Grain
The important point is, of course, that these organizations say they have not changed their views about asking for cash advances. I note, also, that on March 12, 1957, the three western Canadian wheat pools met in Ottawa and asked the government in clause 5 of the resolution they passed for a reduction in the interest rate on grain loans. There has never been any change on the part of organized agriculture in its demand for cash advances. They probably feel, as we hon. members of this house feel, that if this government does not see fit to provide for cash advances through legislation they will take advantage of the loans, because I can tell this house that there are a lot of desperate farmers in western Canada to whom a loan will be necessary if they are to put in their crops this spring.
Again, in order to show the house that the policy of the wheat pools has not changed, I have here the wheat pool policy of 1956, and I just want to quote one paragraph from it:
The current problem of a shortage of farm cash was considered as soon as the annual meeting opened. The delegates went on record in favour of a system of cash advances against farm-stored grain to be paid out by the Canadian wheat board through elevator companies with the federal government assuming the interest on loans involved.
This was given top priority in the agenda of the convention, which indicates that it is a very important matter to the western pool organizations. That policy has not changed, nor has the interprovincial farm union council changed its attitude on cash advances.
This was presented to the government at a meeting in Ottawa on February 19, 1957, and clause 7 of their recommendations reads as follows:
That a permanent system of cash advances be established on the basis recommended in previous submissions, in order that farmers will have the means to meet their annual obligations-also, that provision be made for accelerated depreciation on grain storage buildings built by farmers.
Last year the interprovincial farm union council indicated in their brief what they were asking for and this is what they had to say about cash advances for grain, as found at page 14:
For several years there has been a growing need for some system of interim financing for farmers who find themselves financially embarrassed, while they have harvested a good crop of grain. As a solution to the problem, the interprovincial farm union council during the past months, has strongly advocated a system of cash advances on farm-stored grain through our grain marketing agency, with the federal government absorbing the interest and administration charges.
It is probably not well known among eastern members of parliament but under the operations of the Canadian wheat board the

farmer has been footing the bill at every step in the marketing of his grain. The farmer pays from the time the grain goes into the elevator. If the grain is kept in a commercial or pool elevator, immediately the cost of that storage comes off the final payment to the farmer. When the grain is moved by box car to the lakehead, to Winnipeg, the freight is all charged to the farmer. The cost of every step in the movement of farm grain is charged to the farmer.
It is interesting to point out too that when we talk about an initial price of $1.40 a bushel for farm wheat that is the price at the lake-head or at the Vancouver export point and all freight charges to that point are deducted from what is paid to the farmer. In addition, there is the fact that very seldom is his wheat graded No. 1. Therefore the problem is that the income of the farmer has dropped over the last three or four years while his costs have risen and he has been caught in such a cost-price squeeze, plus the fact that he has had low marketing quotas, that he is in a desperate position in trying to finance his operations.
I think this legislation is rather an insult to the farmers of western Canada who are trying to do a good job, and, incidentally, have done a good job. They are in no position except to agree with the type of marketing we have. The problem of selling the grain rests with the federal government, and I believe we would have got rid of a lot more grain if the government had adopted some of the proposals we in this group have advocated over the years such as barter trade and taking more local currency for our exports of grain.
As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) agrees with that, or he did in 1953 because he is reported in the Moose Jaw Times-HeralcL of July 2, 1953 as having said:
Mr. Howe must assume a large amount of responsibility for the loss of Canada's traditional markets in Britain for farm products. Actually he has mishandled the trade portfolio in a way that could only spell ultimate tragedy to thousands of western farmers.
We feel that if the government would undertake some of the plans which the United States government has undertaken through the Commodity Credit Corporation such as barter trade deals it would be a great help. One significant deal made by the Commodity Credit Corporation was with Brazil. Over the next four years Brazil has agreed to take 18,000 tons of United States wheat in exchange for Brazilian commodities. The federal government has seemed to shy away from that type of agreement.
It was with some satisfaction that I heard the minister announce in the house that

Poland has been given a credit and no doubt will be buying more wheat from Canada on an extended credit basis. I am very happy to see that the government is moving in the direction which some of us on this side of the house have been advocating over the years.
There are some features of cash advances compared with bank loans which I should like to bring to the attention of the house. First of all, the farmer would be entitled to a cash advance. He would be able to go to the bank and would not have to depend on the decision of the banker with respect to whether or not he was credit-worthy. He would not have to make commitments as he does under this legislation and he would be entitled to a loan. I favour the suggestion of the interprovincial farm union council that the farmer should be allowed up to $3,000 or $4,000 by way of a loan. I have never been in favour of having the government try to underwrite types of farming which might be described as syndicate farming or big operations, but I do think it would be of advantage to all of Canada to have a program which would sustain the family farm and allow the farmer to be able to pay his bills, thus sustaining the local merchants.
As far as the repayment of cash advances is concerned, it would be almost automatic. When the farmer's grain was sold the sale would be recorded in his permit book at the elevator and therefore repayment would be almost automatic. I have already put forward some of the arguments against bank loans. I have mentioned that if farmers who need money are not credit-worthy they will probably go to a bank and be turned down even in spite of this legislation. Another factor is that in Saskatchewan alone there are 1,100 marketing points and only 350 chartered bank offices. That means in many cases that the farmer who wants to get a loan has to travel 50 to 60 miles, meet a banker whom he probably does not know and make an application for a loan. It is understandable that no great use has been made of this legislation over the past two years. The reason is not wholly that the farmers do not need money. The fact is that the whole operation of this legislation makes it difficult for the farmer to obtain a loan.
I believe that at some point we have got to see to it that the farmer is entitled, the same as any other worker in the country, to payment for the work he has done and there must be some system by which he can get an advance on his grain. Some members went to Washington and examined the system in that country. I think it has tremendous advantages over the proposal contained in the legislation or over the system whereby the
Grain
farmer must wait until he has delivered his grain to the Canadian wheat board to receive the initial payment.
In the United States the farmer delivers his grain to the Commodity Credit Corporation when the corporation calls for it. If the farmer cannot deliver it immediately it is harvested he is allowed to put it in proper storage and he can get an advance on it representing about 90 per cent of parity.
Finally, I say that the minister cannot muddy the waters in the fight for cash advances by saying that the farm organizations have in any way changed their demands for such advances and are now ready to accept bank loans. Nothing could be further from the truth. I am suggesting that there are different ways by which cash advances can be made to the farmers which would in no way jeopardize the Canadian wheat board. I have said before and I repeat that it would be very simple for the federal government to make funds available to the Canadian wheat board so that when the farmer went to the bank and asked for an advance the advance would be one made by the Canadian wheat board. When wheat was delivered to the elevator it would be entered in the farmer's permit book and this would pay back 50 per cent of his loan. The other 50 per cent of the proceeds from the sale of the wheat he would receive in cash and he would continue on that basis until the loan was repaid.
So, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the representations made on behalf of this group will not be taken in this house as an indication that we are asking for a handout for the western farmer. We are asking for simple justice. I do hope that the hon. members for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Mang) and Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer), as well as others, will join us in our long fight for action to obtain a little bit of simple justice for the western farmer. I move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce):
That Bill No. 263 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide a permanent system of cash advances on farm stored grain.

speechtext:
During the discussions which took place on the resolution which preceded the introduction of this bill, on several occasions we in this group pointed out many reasons why we were opposed to this particular measure. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) introduced the resolution to the committee, he pointed out that the resolution had received the support of the farm organizations of western Canada, the three wheat pools of western Canada and the United grain

Grain
growers. He pointed out that these organizations had not only endorsed the principle which he proposed to place in the bill, but had also recommended to him the exact terms which would be included in the bill.
This morning I received in the mail a copy of the latest edition of the "Alberta Wheat Pool Budget", which was printed in Calgary on Friday, March 22. Apparently the "Wheat Pool Budget" is not quite so enthusiastic over the terms of this bill as the Minister of Trade and Commerce would like us to believe. On March 22, they had this to say:
The new measure would answer two of the main criticisms of previous legislation-
They mean the maximum amount of the loan, which would be increased from $1,500 to $3,000, and secondly that the loan would be made available to the farmers in the early fall under the new legislation when it had not been made available in the early fall under the previous legislation. The article goes on to say this:
However, a third main objection that the interest rate at 5 per cent was too high has not been met.
I would take it from this statement in this wheat pool budget that the Alberta wheat pool had not endorsed all the terms of the bill which has been introduced, even though the minister says that they had. The "Wheat Pool Budget" goes on to say this:
While the rate of interest will not be announced until later there has been nothing to indicate that it will be lowered.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, it has been indicated in this house on more than one occasion there is a very definite indication the rate of interest will be raised.
The wheat pools of western Canada have urged that the interest rate be lowered claiming that loans of this nature are not inflationary. In most cases the money secured is used to pay debts already contracted and not to buy consumer goods.
Borrowing is not a solution to the prairie farmers' problem today but for many it is a necessity when they cannot market their grain. They should not be forced to pay large interest charges on top of their many other expenses. The wheat pools contend that the interest on loans made under provisions of this act should be no higher than that paid by the Canadian wheat board on the money it borrows to carry grain.
I felt that in this statement the Alberta Wheat Pool has been very definite in its criticism of this particular legislation. It is pointed out that the farmers of western Canada should not be asked to pay a high rate of interest on the money which they are forced to borrow, through no fault of their own but because of the faulty marketing policies that have been pursued down through the years by our present government.
We in this group are still of the opinion that this is the wrong type of legislation to

be introduced at this session. This legislation is inadequate and unfair to the farmers of western Canada. We feel that the only suitable answer to this problem of surplus grain in western Canada is a system of cash advances on farm stored grain. This has been our stand before and it will continue to be our stand until the government gets busy and moves grain out of the west and places it in the hands of the people in the world who need it.
The minister pointed out that farm organizations had failed to bring forth an alternative plan to this system of loans. I want to ask you, Mr. Speaker, and through you the Minister of Trade and Commerce, this question. Whose responsibility is it to introduce legislation? Surely, the minister does not intend to tell us that his government failed to introduce legislation dealing with cash advances just because the farm organizations of western Canada failed to reach complete agreement in every detail of a proposed scheme. This particular bill is known as the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act. Now, the word "interim" means just one thing, temporary. The bill had the same title last year and was an interim financing act, a temporary measure. I submit that the situation which makes this bill necessary will continue and will not be capable of being classed as temporary if this government, or the government which replaces it, pursues the same marketing policies as those being pursued by this government today. Why has the government failed to advance a permanent, positive policy which would ensure those engaged in all phases of agriculture a just return for their labour? Why are the grain farmers still to be called upon by this government to finance the surplus grain we have in Canada?
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of western Canada made a limited use of this legislation last year. They made use of it because they were forced to do so, not because they wanted to do so. They had to go to the banks and borrow because they could not market their grain and receive cash returns. It is true also that in my own province of Alberta many farmers, through government policy, have been forced to sell their wheat at a greatly reduced price in order to get money. I know of instances where wheat of good quality has been sold for 65 cents per bushel. This legislation with which we are dealing now was of no value to the farmer who had to go out and sell his wheat at that greatly reduced price. Upon many occasions we in this group had made suggestions to the government as to how the surplus grain problem could be

handled. We have suggested, for example, the construction of permanent, government-owned terminals. We have asked that the policy of off-site storage be continued and extended.
I was somewhat amused, Mr. Speaker, when I read a report of the activities of a Liberal candidate in the province of Alberta in the wheat pool budget of March 15. Here is the short article as it appears in this particular budget:
Dr. Gordon Burton, farmer-economist and Liberal candidate for the Macleod riding-
I might point out that the Macleod riding is very capably and efficiently represented at the present time. I continue:
-in the coming election, suggests that the federal government should put up temporary bins with a capacity of 75 million bushels as a means of coping with the large stocks of grain that have accumulated in the prairie provinces.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I wish to submit that that is not a new suggestion. We in this group, and other groups on this side of the house, have suggested to the government many types of emergency measures that could be taken. However, we have always impressed upon the government the fact that something of a permanent nature must be done to enable the farmers of western Canada to receive their fair share of the national income.
This particular proposal made by a Liberal candidate in the province of Alberta is not new; it is not one that has been adopted by the present Liberal government, even though it had been suggested to it. To me, this statement of this Liberal candidate simply means that even Liberal candidates in western Canada recognize the fact that this government has failed to deal efficiently with the surplus grain problem and has forced the farmers of western Canada to carry this burden.
This government has failed to adopt marketing policies which would induce importing countries to buy more grain from Canada. It still refuses to accept the currency of other lands; it still refuses to engage in barter deals, and so forth. The government has refused to accept recommendations made by the farm organizations and by members on this side of the house to institute a system of cash advances on farm-stored grain; nor will the government agree to construct permanent terminal storage space or expand the policy of off-site storage. This bill, Mr. Speaker, is the government's only solution and it is definitely inadequate to meet the situation.
In reading the Ottawa Journal last evening, Mr. Speaker, I was very much struck with the report contained in that particular paper
Grain
of the reaction of certain people in Nova Scotia to the remarks which were said to have been made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair). The Minister of Fisheries is reported as having said:
There is "no point in subsidizing an industry merely for the sake of providing employment".
The Minister of Fisheries was dealing with the coal industry. Does he not know that the agricultural industry is also a depressed industry and that 16 per cent of the people of Canada who are engaged in agriculture receive less than 7 per cent of the national income? Surely, no one will argue that the majority of the farmers of Canada are prosperous. Are we to accept that the government policy, which was enunciated by the Minister of Fisheries, to the the effect that all uneconomic industries, which I assume would include agriculture, must eventually be closed down? In closing, Mr. Speaker, I submit that if the government continues to pursue the policies, or the lack of policies, that it has had in regard to agriculture over the next few years, it will not have to close down the agricultural industry because the farmers themselves, of their own accord, will be forced to stop doing business.

may I submit it strikes me that the amendment that has been moved is in the form of an alternative proposal. Perhaps the hon. member who has moved the amendment has overlooked the fact that what is before the house is not the act that is cited as the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act, 1956; it is an act to amend it, and it is amending it only in this particular, namely, the one relating to extension. The hon. member for Calgary North.

Mr. Speaker, I spoke on this legislation at considerable length when it was at the resolution stage and made my position and that of this party quite clear in regard to it. Therefore, I see no purpose to be served by repeating the arguments that I made at that time that were, as a matter of fact, to a large extent a repetition of the arguments I made a year before when this legislation was first introduced. Therefore, I do not propose to speak at length in regard to this measure.

Grain
I must say also that both last year and this year the position of this party in regard to the matter has been made so clear that I was quite at a loss to understand the somewhat snide remarks which were made by the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) in regard to the speech made by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) at the start of the second reading of this bill. The hon. member for Eglinton, as I think the hon. member for Moose Mountain knows, is the man in this party who particularly looks after matters pertaining to trade and commerce, and as this particular legislation comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce and is in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I think it was very much in order that the hon. member for Eglinton should have spoken on the measure. As a matter of fact, he spoke on it very well and very sensibly. The idea of trying to make rather nasty innuendoes about his having become the chief farm spokesman of the party, and things of that sort, I think were in very poor taste indeed.
As far as the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Moose Mountain is concerned, it is practically the same amendment which I myself moved last year when second reading of this legislation was up for consideration. Under those circumstances, of course, I think it must be quite clear that the members of this party will support the amendment. Essentially, I have risen in my place only to make my position in regard to the amendment clear.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would you like to hear a few words now on the propriety of this amendment? I noted what you said a few moments ago as to the bill that is now before us, it being a bill which amends a statute passed in 1956. It seems to me, sir, that cognizance has to be taken of the fact that unless the bill now before the house is passed the statute that was passed in 1956 expires. In other words, what is before the house, though you technically referred to it

as an amending bill, would continue in effect a statute which otherwise would expire.
The purpose of my colleague's amendment is to state that in our view the bill proposed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce should not be read a second time; in other words, should not be passed. We propose an alternative to the proposition of extending legislation which otherwise would expire. That alternative, of course, is the one spelled out in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough).
We contend that our authority for moving an amendment of this kind is contained in a citation which no doubt is open on your lap right now, citation No. 657 in Beauchesne's third edition, which says:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction, or prosecution:	or otherwise opposed to its progress; or
seeking further information in relation to the bill by committees, commissioners, the production of papers or other evidence or the opinion of judges.
Then there follow two or three citations that develop the point and make it clear that an amendment of this kind must imply opposition to the motion for second reading and must state some alternative. They also make it clear that an amendment of this kind cannot anticipate amendments which could be made to the main bill if that bill got into committee.
It is our contention, sir, that the government's bill and the proposition in my hon. friend's amendment relate to the same subject, namely the needs of the farmers in western Canada, but that they offer solutions to that problem which are quite separate and distinct.
The proposal in the bill put forward by the minister is that legislation which would otherwise die be continued for another year, legislation which guarantees loans made by banks to farmers. The alternative proposal put forward by my colleague is that instead there should be introduced legislation to deal with this matter by means of establishing a permanent system of cash advances on farm stored grain. There have been many instances of amendments of this kind being moved. I suppose the score is about even; about half of them have been allowed and about half of them have been refused. It seems to me, however, that this amendment is in the category of the kind that have been allowed in that it presupposes opposition to the main motion. It is also in that category because its substance is in the same general

field and yet proposes a solution which is different from that proposed by the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rather than the government arguing through the minister that this legislation was not desirable from the government's point of view the minister based the reason for opposing it on the fact that it had not been supported by farmers in general and in particular by the farm organizations of western Canada.
Looking at what the minister said on March 14 it appears he bases his whole argument for introducing this amending bill on the fact that the proposals contained therein had been agreed to by farm organizations in western Canada.
He went on to say-if I may be permitted to paraphrase his words-that he was very happy to be able to introduce a bill which had the wholehearted support of farm organizations in western Canada. He went on to say, as reported at page 2196 of Hansard:
We were asked to enact this legislation by every farm organization in western Canada.
Later on the minister had this to say:
This resolution just deals with one matter, and that is the matter of the unanimous request from every prairie farm organization.
During the resolution stage I placed on the record a copy of the telegram which had been sent to the minister by the prairie farm organizations and which said in effect that they were not happy with what was being proposed in the amendment, that nothing short of cash advances would satisfy the

Grain
needs of the western farmer. However, believing they were not going to get cash advances at this session of parliament they set out certain recommendations and according to the minister's statement those left the impression that the present amendment contained all the things requested by the farm organizations. That is not borne out by the facts. I am not going to place the telegram on the record but I should like to indicate what was recommended by the farm organizations. The points they suggested to the minister should be in the amendment in lieu of cash advances were as follows:
That the basis for loans be set at $4 per specified acre up to a maximum of 800 acres.
That the time for advancement of loans be set ahead to September 1.
That credit unions and treasury branches be empowered to advance loans.
That interest rates be as low as possible and in any event not higher than that paid by Canadian wheat board.
In answer to those requests we have the minister's statement that these organizations wanted larger bank loans made available, $3,000 instead of $1,400. I submit that they asked for nothing of the kind. They asked for $4 per acre up to a maximum of 800 acres. There is no similarity between that request and what we find now in the innocuous amendment contained in Bill No. 86. When a farmer applies for a bank loan he is not asked how many cultivated acres he has, he is asked how many bushels of wheat he has, and then the loan is calculated on the basis of 8 bushels per acre up to a maximum now of $3,000.
I would like to suggest to the parliamentary assistant that he should table the reply of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the telegram received from the farm organizations. We understand that there was a reply and I think in fairness to the house it should be tabled. I believe it would be most revealing.
Getting back to the matter of the increase from $1,500 to $3,000 as set out in the amendment, I have done a little calculating and I should like someone, possibly the parliamentary assistant, to prove to me just how the average farmer, the farmer whom the minister said last year he was setting out to help, is going to benefit from this increase from $1,500 to $3,000.
Take a half-section farmer, and there are a good many of them in western Canada, and give him 300 cultivated acres which is certainly not stretching the point. When he markets his unit of 300 bushels he can only qualify for a loan of $900. On the other hand, if you take a three-quarter section farmer and give him 440 acres out of the

480 acres, with which I do not think anyone will quarrel, the largest amount he -could possibly borrow under the amended act would be $1,460. The average of those two loans is $1,160. We know from past experience and from figures placed on Hansard by the minister that the average of the loans made under the present legislation was only $764. It is impossible to expect that this amendment which raises the amount from $1,500 to $3,000 is going to help the farmer whom the minister was so anxious to help when he introduced the bill last year.
Nothing is said about interest rates. We know what has happened during the past few months; we know that interest rates have been increased by three-quarters of one per cent to the elevator companies which are handling and marketing the farmers' grain.
That simply means that the farmer is going to get $2 million less in his final payment when he receives it for the wheat which he markets. Over the past few months there have been several increases. The government has said that these increases in interest rates are made to fight inflation, but what they are doing here is simply to take away with the one hand $11 million in increased interest rates to the elevator companies which must go out and borrow tremendous amounts of money in order to market and handle the farmers' grain. Those costs are passed on to the wheat board and the wheat board charges them back in the final payment to the farmer. The result is that the farmer's purchasing power is cut further and further. In this amendment we are faced with the fact that interest rates can be set at the discretion of the governor in council and those would be the rates the banks would charge on these loans. We are dubious about this. We believe that interest rates are going to be increased.
I was disturbed at the argument used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to discredit bank loans. He said that the businessmen of this country are anxious to see cash advance legislation introduced, that they have an ulterior motive. I submit that the small businessman in western Canada is part and parcel of the agricultural set-up. It adds nothing to the argument of the minister to suggest that it is the businessman who is trying to force the hand of the farmer in asking for cash advances. The businessman is placed in an untenable position. He must provide credit at no cost. It is a great embarrassment for the farmer customer to have to ask for it and we know it is a financial strain on the businessman to give that credit.
We hope the government will reconsider this legislation and will accept the amendment

2705 moved. We are convinced that the legislation before us has no value and will be of no value to the farmers who are in great need. Therefore we hope the government will give further consideration to the implementation of cash advances as one way in which this situation can be remedied.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do hope the amendment will not be ruled out of order, because it does give us an opportunity of indicating exactly what we want, and of indicating it in an active way by a vote. The amendment as it now reads, if it should be decided that it is in order, is:
That the bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide a permanent system of cash advances on farm-stored grain.
That is what we in this group want. We don't want to run a farmer into more debt when he has assets he wants to dispose of. We say he should be able to receive cash for the grain which the wheat board must eventually take from him.
Mr. Speaker, let me just pose a question or two for the sake of provoking some thought. Why is such legislation as this thought by the government to be needed? There is only one answer to that, namely that the farmers are in straitened financial circumstances. All right. That poses another question. Why are the farmers in straitened financial circumstances? Have they been unsuccessful in their farming? I don't think so.
The fact of the matter is that the farmers of western Canada have been extremely successful. They have been so successful in the operation of their farms that they have been able to bring about these surpluses in grain, or what we call these surpluses of grain. So we find successful farmers, now, who have no cash. That is the position. Is that any fault of their own? I believe the fault lies in the fact that the only selling agency through which a farmer can market his grain has not been able to dispose of this wheat.
I am not going to be too harsh with regard to the Canadian wheat board, because we recently read that the Canadian wheat board has exceeded, in its sales, the amount it has been able to dispose of in previous years. Nevertheless we have what might be termed a surplus and, on the other hand, we have what might be said to be a starving world. That is the picture. We are told by competent authorities that nearly half the world, including some iron curtain countries, is still at a starvation level. These are the nations that need to be fed; these are the nations that need our grain. Yet the Canadian wheat board has not been able to dispose of our wheat in such
Grain
a fashion that these starving nations could be fed with the vast abundance of grain that we in Canada have produced.
That poses another question. Why is this so? Once again the responsibility must be placed upon the shoulders of this present government, because they have not instituted financial policies capable of moving this grain to the countries which need it. As my colleague from Battle River-Camrose has said on a number of occasions, and as I myself and a number of others in this group have pointed out, the fact that the government will not change its financial policy and accept foreign currency for our exports is one reason why we have not been able to dispose of our surplus.
I would just like to say a word with respect to this so-called surplus. I have mentioned on several occasions, and sometimes taken the chance of being misunderstood, that we do not have a surplus of grain. That, of course, is hard to put over to people who may drive along our country highways and find grain piled up in the middle of fields. But, as I point out, the term "surplus" is a relative term. When we use the term "surplus" we must ask "surplus to what?". If we say it is a surplus over the amount the Canadian wheat board has been able to dispose of, then of course we have to say that we have a surplus. But if we ask ourselves whether it is a surplus over what the world needs in order to be fed, then I say we have no surplus.
Mr. Speaker, I ask another question. Sometimes questions provoke a good deal of thought. This question is a pertinent one. What is land for if it is not to grow crops? My hon. friend from Bow River says land can be used to bury you in.

I am glad my hon. friend qualified that statement.
What is land for, if it is not for the purpose of growing foodstuffs? Why does a farmer go out and plant his grain if he does not expect to get a yield? I notice in the Gordon report they say one reason for the surplus of grain we have in this country is that over the past number of years we have had exceptionally good weather. I am not so foolish as to attribute the surpluses to the weather. I am one of those who do not believe that nature plays very many tricks; eventually nature can be relied upon. Imagine a farmer going out and putting in his crop and then, during the summer months, when we have had fine weather, rain and sunshine, going out and looking over his crops and

Private Bills-Divorce
finding that there is a prospect of reaping 30, 40 or even 50 bushels to the acre-imagine him turning away in sorrow and saying, "Oh, my goodness, I hope this good weather does not continue, because if it does I am going to have too much grain."
We would say such a man would be very foolish. The fact is that the farmer is there to raise crops. He hopes he will get fine weather and a good yield.
There is only one marketing agency through which he can market his wheat. We are all in favour of the wheat board because it has done an admirable job for the farmer. Nevertheless it is a government agency, and the only agency through which a wheat farmer can market his crop. The farmer has done his job by raising the crop. Now he cannot dispose of it; he has no cash, and the government turns round and says, "Well, we know our agency is the only agency which will take your wheat, but we won't take it because we have too much now." The farmer says, "What am I going to do?" and the reply he gets is, "We are sorry, we cannot help you; but we will submit some legislation whereby you will be able to borrow money from the bank, provided you pay the cost of it." This is tantamount to the farmer paying interest on his own grain. He is in the unfortunate position of having no cash because he has done an excellent job.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that it is five o'clock.

subtopic: JOSEPH RICARDO BOUZIANE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this particular case, the petition for relief of Joseph Ricardo Bouziane, was heard before subcommittee No. 3 of the other place. The chairman' of the committee was Senator Cameron from Alberta, and the other members of the committee were Senator Gershaw of Alberta, Senator Hodges of British Columbia and Senator Smith of the province of Nova Scotia. According to the evidence of this young man who appeared before them, at the time of his marriage he was 18 or 19 years of age. At the time he appeared before the committee he was 20 years of age. He is a member of the Roman Catholic faith and so is his wife. He is a mechanic by trade.
[Mr. Hansell.l
The record shows that this young man was married on August 27, 1955. His wife gave birth to a child on December 19, 1955. He says their difficulties began about three months after the wedding, in other words around November 19, 1955. This means that their difficulties began about a month before the first child was born. In the transcript of the evidence I find the following;
Q. Relate to the honourable members of this committee what happened after your marriage? A. Well, it began about three months after the marriage.
Q. What did? A. She started going out and we started having little fights. About three months after the wedding-
I repeat that he again emphasizes that the time was about three months after the wedding, which was one month before the child was born.
-I used to work very much at night till about 11 o'clock in the evening and come home, and many times she was not there and I had a hard time to find out where she was during the evening.
Q. Do you mean a hard time by talking to her or by seeking her out? A. Talking to her and seeking her out.
Q. She would not give any account where she was? A. No, she wouldn't. Then I started to follow her around and see what was going on and find out; she was going out with different men, and quite often-
Q. How did you find that? A. Some friends told me, and I also followed them myself.
It is rather incredible that a month before the birth of her first child a woman would begin to go out with other men, and that she would refuse to account for her absence when asked to do so by her husband. He testified further that when the baby was four months old his wife left the house. That was on March 18, 1956. He says he did not know where she had gone, and in the evidence I find the following:
Q. Continue relating to the honourable members of this committee your personal observations. A. On March 18, 1956 she left the house and she came back a couple of days later just to get some clothes and leave again.
Q. Where was the baby in the meantime? A. The baby she took with her at the time. At first I didn't know where she was living, and finally I got a phone call from her she needed money, and she was living at her sister's place, and I decided to give money for the child. I was paying $10 a week from March 20 approximately until July-
I would simply like to comment on the fact that she left him on March 18 and he did not know where she was living, but nevertheless he started to pay her $10 a week only two days after she left him. It is hardly believable that he did not know where she was living and would yet be paying $10 a week for the maintenance of the youngster. Then he goes on:
-and then in July the child was very sick and she brought it over to my father's who is a doctor in Montreal, to take care of him. We had to send

him to the hospital for a couple of days, and brought it back and the child has been with me ever since.
Q. Since that date that the child was brought back has she been to live with you? A. No, definitely not, she has not been back to see the child or anything.
In the first place we feel that since this young man was married at such a very early age and was only married for such a short time-in fact he was only married a little over a year when he petitioned the other place for a divorce-obviously there was not too much of an effort at reconciliation. In the second place, it is very hard to believe that a young woman will run out on her husband, take the baby with her and because of the baby's illness bring it back so the husband's father, who is a doctor, can look after the baby and then desert the baby completely and never once come back to see her child.
I notice that again the detective agency is the Reliable detective agency. Mr. Etheridge, who I understand is the owner, is one of the witnesses. Mr. Etheridge is only 41 years of age, and it is most regrettable that a young man of 41 who has so much of his life ahead of him should be wasting his life in enterprises such as this. The detective agency should be subjected to the most thorough investigation.

Mr. Speaker, I should advise the house that this is the 207th divorce bill to reach the House of Commons this session, and I understand there are ahout 200 more on the way.
I would like to make a few comments about the evidence supplied to members of the committee in connection with this case. The petitioner in this action was married in 1941 and has a child 14 years of age. The questioning in the other committee, in part, was as follows:
Q. And did you obtain your final judgment in separation? A. Yes. I did.
Q. Were you granted custody of the child? A. Yes,
I was.
Q. Now, since that period of time has your husband supported you and the child? A. No, he has not.
Q. Have you been working? A. Yes, I have.
Q. Have you lived with your husband since January, 1946?
A. No, I have not.
Q. When did you consult your attorneys about this present petition?
A. In November, 1956.
The following questions, I think, are extremely important:
Q. Is there any collusion or arrangement between you and your husband to obtain this divorce?
A. No, there is not.
Q. Have you in any way connived with this-
-Miss so and so-
.-to take your husband away from you so that you could present this petition?
A. No, I have not.
Q. Is there any condonation or forgiveness on your part?
A. No.
The only witnesses called in this particular case were the petitioner, the husband, and the corespondent. The husband was called and gave his full name, age, address and occupation. He was asked if he could identify the

lady sitting on his left, and he was able to identify her as his wife. He was asked if he knew another lady and he replied that he did. The questioning was as follows:
Q. How long have you known her?
A. About three years.
Q. Are you living with her today?
A. That is right.
Q. And are you still living with her as man and wife?
A. Yes.
He proceeded to indicate where he is living with the young lady in question. I should explain, of course, that before he was asked these questions he was addressed by the chairman of the committee, His Honour Senator Golding, as follows:
Witness, in compliance with the evidence act, R.S.O., 1950, chapter 119, section 8, I have to give you this warning. This is a very sad case. I see there is some humour expressed in the house, Mr. Speaker, but there are some people who view these unhappy marriages with a good deal of concern.
I rise at this time because, as I say, I feel this is an unfortunate situation. In the first instance, the young woman who is the petitioner in this case has applied for a divorce, I suppose of necessity, of course, because she and her husband have proved to be completely incompatible. The petition is by Pauline Margaret Patricia Sylvester McLean, and she is seeking divorce from Maurice Allan McLean.
She married at the age of 15 or 16, apparently in the year 1950. Within two years, according to the evidence presented in the other place, there were differences between her and her husband. She was questioned with regard to this situation by one of the senators, as follows:
Q. When did you quit living with your husband?
A. In 1952.
Q. Would you please state why?
A. He was not behaving properly and he was drinking very heavily, and he was seeing other women.
Apparently the first act of infidelity took place shortly after they were married. I would like to point out that there have been two children of this marriage. Donald, aged 6 and Michael aged 4. I am certain that since every hon. member of this house is concerned about the situation facing parliament with regard to having to deal with these divorce cases, there will be particular concern about this case where two small children are involved.
Apparently the husband had been sending this young woman certain sums of money, recently at least, without a court order having been obtained. Immediately after the couple were separated the wife took her husband to court in order to force him to make some contribution to her and her children's keep. But at the present time, apparently, as far as I have been able to gather from the evidence, the husband is now giving some assistance to his wife merely out of concern for the children and not as the result of a court order.

Reading the evidence in this case I feel, Mr. Speaker, that one would have to be presumptuous to accept some of the evidence given in trying to establish adultery. It does seem to me an indication that the hon. members of the other place must surely have come to the conclusion that here was a marriage which had proved to be unsuccessful, that no good could come from trying to resolve the difficulties of those concerned, and that a divorce should therefore be agreed to. There was no investigating officer. A young man, a friend of the petitioner, was apparently the person who drove with the petitioner to a motel, following the petitioner's husband.
After the lights went out in the motel, according to the evidence, they entered the motel. The door was not locked. They proceeded to the bed and found these two people in bed. Apparently there was no word spoken between any of the four people present. I can only come to the conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that here is a case which would suggest that the petitioner as well as the respondent were quite agreed that a divorce should be obtained, and were quite happy about it.
However, I do think this case calls attention to the fact that in Canada this situation of broken marriages has reached the extent of being a national tragedy, and though we are dealing at the moment exclusively with this bill, it is proper to suggest that we should have some type of pre-marriage counselling by competent people, particularly of young people entering marriage, by means of which we might dispose of some of these problems we have to face in parliament by reason of these divorce petitions arising in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland, which have to be heard by this assembly.
